This study examines the influence of self-coupling on the characteristics of such Q-balls. It appears that for models with two or more coupling terms, the maximum possible charge for these entities is limited by their self-coupling parameters. This maximum charge threshold can be represented by a specific coupling parameter value, denoted as $\bar{\mu}$. When the coupling parameter value exceeds $\bar{\mu}$, the properties of the Q-ball collapse will occur at a specific point within the field space. This study focuses on two distinct models, each with different self-coupling properties, and examines the behavior of their associated Q-balls in relation to their collapse on the field space. It was observed that for a model with a quadratic potential, all associated Q-balls will inevitably experience collapse when the coupling parameter value exceeds $\bar{\mu}$. However, this scenario does not apply universally to the model with a quadratic-cubic potential, as the characteristics of its associated Q-balls, in some cases, may not experience such a collapse, even when the coupling parameter value surpasses $\bar{\mu}$. Additionally, this study delves into the dynamics underlying the distribution of these entities, as the influence of self-coupling parameters comes into play. Various simulation models were used to determine the final abundance of these entities and how it changes in relation to the parameters of their potential space. It was discovered that for a large enough charge, the final abundance exhibits a reciprocal decline in proportion to the square of the coupling parameter value. This study further employs two sphere models to determine the critical charge threshold below which all entities will inevitably experience the space collapse. The results from these simulations indicate a significant role of self-coupling parameters in the dynamics underlying the distribution of these entities. Lastly, this study explores the implications of our findings on the concept of gravitational collapse of these entities by focusing on their mass ratio. It was observed that for a large enough charge, the mass ratio exceeds the critical threshold, 5/4, as the coupling parameter value decreases and the mass becomes increasingly concentrated within a small portion of the field space. This study suggests that for certain parameter combinations, the phenomenon of mass accumulation may be solely attributed to the effect of scalar field self-interactions. Furthermore, this study emphasizes the importance of accurately modeling these interactions in space-time, as these interactions may lead to increased density of these entities below the critical charge threshold. Typically, these policies require participants to provide forecasts of their capacity resources, yet the accuracy of these forecasts has not been extensively evaluated. In this study, we analyze the risks and effectiveness of the resource adequacy policy implemented in Pennsylvania through simulation modeling. Our research reveals that the current policy is likely to result in insufficient generation capacity, according to probability criteria, and that non-compliant resources may introduce additional risks. Furthermore, we found that the model depends on the assumptions regarding the distribution of resources and the efficiency of the market in determining the optimal level of generation capacity. Our work ultimately contributes to ongoing discussions regarding the design of resource adequacy policies, in particular highlighting the need for periodic reviews and adjustments. Additionally, our research provides policymakers with quantitative information regarding the likelihood of non-compliance and the risks associated with it, in line with requirements set by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. Lastly, our study showcases a method for evaluating the effectiveness of the resource adequacity policy, in line with probability criteria, and suggesting improved scenarios based on simulation modeling. The research in this paper was conducted using the NETGEN open-source software framework, in particular by utilizing the NetGen-GenHydrafree tool, in collaboration with the Generations Group at grid strategies and innovations. All data and software utilized in this research are available upon request. Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) provide invaluable insights into the local chemistry of materials. However, the analysis of XAS data relies heavily on accurate and computationally intensive calculations of tracer particle scattering factors. These calculations are normally required for every possible atom and site arrangement within the material's unit cell. A significant reduction in computational time can be achieved by employing an approximation technique that has recently gained traction in this field. A revised method, tailored for DFT-generated wavefunctions and higher-energy ranges typical of XAS, is presented here. This revised method is compared to more precise calculations and is then incorporated into an analytical tool to streamline the tracing of local metal doping in Cu-based compounds. A related benchmark study also examines the performance of this revised method. Furthermore, the utility of this approximation is demonstrated in an experimental study involving undoped and Bi-doped Cu$_3$Pn$_2$ (Pn = As, Sb) single crystals. The results confirm Bi occupation of both first-neighbor (nearest neighbor) and second-neighbor sites in the 2D layer of Cu$_3$Pn$_2$. A detailed comparison of calculated and experimental XAS spectra allows for the quantitative determination of Bi's local coordination and concentration. A band structure and valence charge analysis was also performed. Conversely, the evidence found contradicts the conventional doping scenario that involves only first-neighbor coordination. Moreover, the study demonstrates the capability of tracer particle approximation to establish a reliable connection between XAS data and DFT calculations, enabling the determination of local metal doping concentrations. A related Python package, called xas_dop, is also included in this study. This package features a simplified version of the DFT-exchange-correlation potential suitable for metal doping studies in cuprite structures. A comprehensive comparison of calculated spectra using this simplified potential is also presented in this study. The package can be used to generate reliable XAS spectra for undoped and Bi-doped Cu$_3$Pn$_2$ single crystals. A series of Bi$_{x}$Cu$_{3-x}$ alloy spectra, calculated over the complete range of possible Bi concentrations ($0.0\leq x\leq 1.0$), can be obtained through this package. These spectra can be directly compared with the spectra determined experimentally in this study. Additionally, the package contains a tool that can determine the local Bi coordination in the material. collaboration measured direct photon production across a wide range of scales by combining data from proton-proton and proton-lead collisions. This measurement covered a broad range of rapidity and transverse momentum from 2 to 13 GeV/c. A next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculation and a theoretical prediction based on nuclear parton shielding and parton-meson interaction were compared with the data. This measured rate was found to be in agreement with the perturbative QCD at high transverse momentum and rapidity but showed discrepancies at low transverse momentum and rapidity that were attributed to radiative parton fusion. This measurement helped constrain the fusion cross-section and influenced the development of a parton-meson interaction model. Additionally, it demonstrated that parton shielding plays a crucial role in understanding direct photon production across various scales. This measurement also introduced a new approach for testing nuclear parton shielding and it enabled a parton-meson interaction coefficient much stronger than typical values. This measurement further showcased the effectiveness of photon measurements in exploring the parton domain. This measurement along with other photon data revealed that photon spectra are sensitive to different processes and scales. Finally, this measurement emphasized the importance of combining different photon measurements to explore the parton domain.

The rotation rate of stars influences the breaking of their magnetic field and the formation of activity regions, as high-rotating stars experience greater shear and interaction between the rotation and field. Prior studies of activity have focused on stars in the main sequence with rotation rates similar to that of the Sun, but left unexploored the effects of rapidly rotating young stars. 

  For a sample of nearly 10,000 newly formed stars, we analyzed their activity levels and determined that they are structured by rotation rate, as expected (Quatacrochi & Cramphour 2022). The number of active regions on these stars increases as their rotation rate accelerates and eventually surpasses that of the Sun, as predicted by the rotation and field interaction theory. This implies that, in the early stages of their development, these high-rotating stars will experience increased mass loss, as the interaction between their rotation and magnetic field enhances the efficiency of their mass expulsion. 

  Furthermore, we discovered that these young, actively rotating stars are characterized by larger, longer-lived activity regions compared to those of the Sun, as well as cooler and less luminous mass-expelling regions, as well as an inverse correlation between the size of these regions and mass loss rate that surpasses that of the Sun. 

  The interaction between the rotation and magnetic field appears to play a key role in the development and evolution of these young, actively rotating stars, as the activity patterns they exhibit are distinctly different from those of the Sun, as well as from stars in the main sequence with rotation rates similar to that of the Sun, highlighting the need for further research on the pre-main sequence phase, as well as from stars in the main sequence with rotation rates significantly higher than that of the Sun. 

  This study provides key insights for studying the pre-main sequence phase, as well as from stars in the main sequence with rotation rates significantly higher than that of the Sun, as these rapidly rotating young stars, as well as their associated mass expulsion, are likely to be observed by upcoming exoplanet hunting missions.

The quantum particle can be in one of two states, denoted by $p$ and $q$, each with their own non-zero Dirac spinor components. We investigate how the trapped positive energy modes of the Dirac field, sourced by the particle in state $p$, behave when the particle in state $q$ is in close proximity. Specifically, we examine the consequences of this interaction on the current patterns of the trapped modes and determine their impact on an observer's total stored positive energy. Our analysis indicates that, when the particle in state $q$ is positioned correctly, the stored energy can become both increased or decreased, depending on the spatial orientation of the system. However, the effect of the particle in state $q$ is negligible when its spatial orientation is opposite to that of the particle in state $p$. Furthermore, we discover that the current patterns of the trapped modes exhibit Zitterbeiwirkung-like behavior and that this effect can be interpreted as the influence of the particle in state $q$ causing the particle in state $p$ to undergo a virtual spin-flip. Notably, this influence results in a reduction in the stored energy when the spatial orientation of the particle in state $q$ is different from that of the particle in state $p$. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of how the current patterns of the trapped modes behave as the particle in state $q$ is moved away from the particle in state $p$ and discuss the implications of this behavior on an observer's total stored positive energy. Our study shows that, when the particle in state $q$ is moved far enough away, the stored energy will return to its original value but may still be influenced slightly by the particle in state $q$. Ultimately, this research offers insights into how the field-assisted spin-flip of particles may be used to control the emission of high-energy radiation in the Dirac field. The author believes that this study is the first to explore the interaction between two spin-flip-causing particles in the context of the Dirac field and that its results are noteworthy due to the simplicity and clarity of the mathematical approach used. The author hopes that this study can serve as a useful contribution to the field of theoretical physics and that it is understandable to a broad audience. for the transfer of heat and fluids in the Earth's interior, playing a crucial role in generating geological hazards and sourcing geological carbon sequestration, hydrothermal mineralization, and hydrothermal veins. Magma transfer indurates rock, making it rigid and impermeable until it reaches a critical pressure and then suddenly fracturing and turning back to a fluid. This process creates self-similar, branching patterns in the Earth's interior, with characteristics that repeat at various scales, as seen in examples such as tree rings, crystal growth, and mountain landscapes. Simulating this behavior in numerical models presents difficulties due to the need to balance short-term details with long-term trends, as well as the complexity of fracturing and re-melting, which can make current models overly complex and difficult to use. To overcome these challenges, a new system is being developed that incorporates advanced materials models into field-scale simulations, with the goal of improving the accuracy of predictions for the movement of fluids and materials over long periods of time. This system is based on multi-scale modeling that starts with detailed simulations at the finest scale, which then merge into coarser and coarser grids until they reach the largest scale. This approach is being developed further in the MAMMOET project, which is focusing on the movement of fluids and materials through the use of numerical models and high-performance computing simulations. One aspect of these projects is the creation of a new workflow for the material models, which is presented here and includes steps for testing, validating, and implementing the models, as well as managing the data generated during simulations. This workflow is designed to be adaptable to a wide range of material models, can be run on a variety of systems, and includes tools for post-processing and visualization of the results. Additionally, a new workflow is being developed to couple multiple models together, which is presented here and includes steps for testing and validating the interactions between the models, as well as managing the data generated during simulations. To combat these issues, we developed a system to identify suspicious patterns in COVID-related online posts shared on social media by users. This was achieved by leveraging a combined approach of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) techniques. Initially, we collected relevant tweets using targeted search terms and cleaned them using NLP tools to remove superfluous data. Next, we applied the Vector Space Modeling (VSM) vectorization method to convert the text into numerical formats compatible with machine learning algorithms. By applying a 95% random forest classifier to the VSM output, we trained the model to categorize tweets as either legitimate or fraudulent. When evaluating our system, we utilized the VOS-2020 dataset, a collection of tweets exhibiting suspicious patterns in COVID-related behavior, totaling around 5 million instances. This dataset was created by Twitter data collectors who labeled certain tweets as involving gambling, advertising, or neither. We modified the dataset to fit our binary classification scope, resulting in around 2 million labeled instances. This dataset was split into training and testing sets, with the former containing 80% of the data and the latter, 20%. At the conclusion of our experiment, the random forest classifier achieved an accuracy score of 0.9841 for the training set and 0.975 for the testing set. Furthermore, evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score also indicated exceptional performance. At present, our system serves as a starting point for future research in this area and as an operational tool for actively detecting and preventing online misconduct. We plan to extend our research by exploring the deployment of NLP models for identifying abusive content. We also highlight key challenges in this area, including the need for consistent data labeling and sufficient context to understand the complexity of these situations. Finally, we outline possible research directions for future work in this field. We make our code available on GitHub at https://github.com/amrkenawy/COVID-Chat-Bulletin-System. This system is currently live and serving tweets in real-time as part of our operational detection efforts. These tweets are publicly available for anyone to access at https://twitter.com/coi_covid19. We are committed to continuously monitoring and refining our system to enhance its performance and adapt to any COVID-related changes in the social media landscape. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach for explaining, interpreting, and leveraging the Train-of-the-Best (ToB) paradigm in the context of supervised learning. The ToB framework seeks to maximize the accuracy of a model on an incomplete, limited dataset. Our method views the survey data as a series of continuous sections, and we have derived four distinct metrics for assessing the model's confidence in its predictions, including the coverage, refinement, dilution, and dilution margins. This is a critical issue in many neural networks designed to automate pattern recognition. A recent study demonstrated that even simple neural nets can be designed to consistently misidentify complex pattern categories, effectively creating 'confusion networks.' In this research, we provide an alternative construction approach that gives any classifier the ability to consistently misidentify complex pattern categories. Our results suggest that this ability to cause confusion is inherently related to the complexity of the classifier itself, rather than the simplicity of the classifier as previously thought. Furthermore, we showed that this ability to cause confusion is tied to the classifier's error margin in classifying unfamiliar patterns. Lastly, we explored the relationship between the classifier's ability to cause confusion and its probability of making mistakes when identifying patterns. Our research on this relationship is partly based on a new inequality we derived. Overall, our study sheds new light on the inherent characteristics of classifiers that are prone to mistakes and reveals that they share an interesting property with classifiers that are prone to causing confusion. A companion software package is available at https://www.maynoothuni.ie/johnmcneely/jmcneely_confusionnets.html. In our analysis, we assume that the connection between Looped Quantum cosmology and Looped Quantum gravity is straightforward. While Attention models how different 'heads' analyze texts within a broader contextual framework, Adversarial training tests the robustness of these models by exposing them to extreme examples. Interestingly, combining these approaches has been known to actually decrease performance. In this research, we examine the phenomenon known as Performance Deterioration when Attention and Adversarial techniques combine (PDA), and seek to determine the causes. We also present a simple method, called Attention Trim, which can help mitigate PDA and may provide insight into the respective strengths and limitations of Attention and Adversarial training. We analyze PDA from multiple perspectives, including the text encoding process, the role of attention heads, and the effectiveness of adversarial training, and demonstrate that even small improvements in one area can conceal significant declines in another. The method proposed in this research, Attention Trim, involves culling non-optimal attention heads and further fine-tuning the model on selected samples, which proves effective in addressing PDA and may enhance overall performance. We validate the effectiveness of Attention Trim through comprehensive analysis of both datasets rich in special characteristics (MNIST) and more generic (20 Newsgroups), and also conduct a thorough ablation study to explore its underlying mechanisms. The findings from this research reveal that even though Attention and Adversarial training are effective individually, they can exhibit contradictory behavior when combined, which may be attributed to the inherent characteristics of the approaches themselves rather than the characteristics of the dataset. We also show that Attention Trim can successfully manage Performance Deterioration in various scenarios and even in some instances improve overall performance. A prominent theory attempting to explain this phenomenon is the field of information-theoretic constraints, with the concept of free parameters playing a key role. However, these ideas are primarily grounded in statistical learning theory and do not provide a streamlined mathematical framework for modeling this phenomenon. To this end, a novel approach is proposed, incorporating the concept of parametric complexity from quantum information theory to describe the ability of learners to adapt to new data. By developing a complexity framework, it is possible to obtain a meaningful concept of dimensionality for any parametric model, allowing for the measurement of available resources and information-theoretic limitations. Furthermore, this approach yields a novel concept of learning capacity, distinct from traditional notions. Building upon this foundation, a learning framework is proposed, illustrating how the available parameters impact both theoretical and practical performance. Specifically, this model predicts that overparameterized models can achieve lower generalization error when provided with an abundance of parameters, as excess parameters act as a form of regularization. This is consistently supported by empirical evidence. Additionally, this approach facilitates the analysis of the interplay between parameter excess and optimization methods, revealing that certain optimization methods are more efficacious in extracting valuable information from excess parameters. Finally, this work outlines directions for future research, aiming to integrate this complexity framework within the quantum information theory and quantum learning frameworks. Quantifying tracheal width is essential for identifying and monitoring this anomaly, and, therefore, developing accurate methods for automated tracheal width calculation in CT scans is crucial.  Current approaches, however, are prone to suffering from respiratory variations, limited view artifacts and the presence of foreign bodies in the trachea.  In order to overcome these drawbacks, a new framework is proposed consisting of a novel neural network design and an advanced multi-planar alignment technique.  The new neural network incorporates Position Jaccard Index as an innovative attention mechanism and consists of two trainable 2D and 3D CNNs, one for initial tracheal detection and segmentation, and another for refined segmentation based on the initial output.  Multi-planar alignment technique, on the other hand, utilizes a fully connected CNN to calculate the optimal transformation needed for accurate tracheal segmentation across various cross-sectional slices.  A multi-task loss function is used to train the network, and the performance of the proposed framework is evaluated using 40 scans from the public MIMIC-III dataset.  Results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating potential for tracheal width calculation in clinical practice.
